newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end up on post-refunding short-cover.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end up on post-refunding short-cover.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed sharply higher in active trade on Thursday as players breathed a sigh of relief after the Treasury's quarterly refunding effort ended, analysts said.
The 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up a full point at 98-11/32 to yield 6.63 percent.

Experts also said many dealers, who were perceived to be holding short positions going into the auctions, rushed back to the market looking to cover their positions during the post-refunding buying spree.
"We saw a nice spark after we made it through the refunding auctions," said John Canavan, Treasury market analyst at Stone and McCarthy Research Associates Inc.

Analysts said players returned to the market after three consecutive sessions of very sluggish trade as the Treasury concluded its three-day refunding effort with the auction of $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds.
The securities were placed with an average yield of 6.640 percent. The bid-to-cover ratio was at 2.42 to one, the highest for this refunding.

Still, analysts said a tail of two basis points signaled some weakness. "Based on the post-auction expectations, it was a weak result," said Lee Youngdahl, vice president at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. Inc.
"We got the tail all the way back to 6.66 (percent) ... It wasn't a terrible result, but it was not a very good one either," Youngdahl added.

But pundits said the mediocre outcome was not enough to hold prices down. "The 30-year auction didn't go specially well, but even that was not enough to hold the market back," Stone and McCarthy's Canavan said.

Analysts said bullishness in the stock market contributed to cheer up money investors as well. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended up 60.81 at 7,022.44 points. The Dow pierced the 7,000 barrier for the first time ever earlier on Thursday.
"People are just getting a general bullish sentiment from a little of carry over from the stock market," said a trader at a major U.S. investment bank.

Analysts said a positive retail sales report for January also provided some underlying support to the Treasury market. Retail sales were up 0.6 percent against a downwardly revised 0.3 percent rise in December.
Wall Street experts in a Reuters poll had expected a 0.7 percent rise in the January retail numbers.

"You still have some decent consumer spending growth going into the first quarter, but it was not quite what was expected. People expected stronger growth," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
The market also took in a drop in jobless claims to 309,000 in the week ended February 8 from a revised 324,000 in the prior week.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down two basis points at 4.99 percent. The six-month bill rate fell five points to 4.99 percent. The year bill rate was off three points at 5.18 percent.

The two-year note closed up 4/32 at 100-4/32, yielding 5.81 percent. The five-year note traded up 9/32 at 100-20/32 to yield 6.10 percent. The ten-year note closed up 16/32 at 99-18/32, yielding 6.31 percent.
